summary_profile.description: Typhoid fever is a serious systemic bacterial infection caused by the bacterium *Salmonella enterica* serovar Typhi. It primarily affects the intestines but can spread throughout the body. The disease is transmitted through the fecal-oral route, usually via contaminated food or water. Without proper treatment, it can lead to life-threatening complications. It remains a significant public health issue in developing countries with poor sanitation. With timely antibiotic treatment, most people recover fully, but untreated cases have a high mortality rate.
common_symptoms: Sustained high fever (39–40°C / 102–104°F) that increases gradually over several days
Constipation (common in adults) or diarrhea (more common in children)
Rose-colored spots (rose spots) on the chest and abdomen (in 30% of cases)
severe_symptoms: Persistent high fever not responding to medication
Confusion, delirium, or altered mental status
Shock (low blood pressure, cold clammy skin)
causes: Salmonella Paratyphi A, B, or C (causes paratyphoid fever — milder form)
Ingestion of food or water contaminated with feces of infected persons
Poor hand hygiene by food handlers (carriers)
Consumption of raw or undercooked food, unpasteurized milk, or contaminated ice
Chronic carriers — people who recover but continue to carry the bacteria in their gallbladder
risk_factors: Living in or traveling to endemic areas (South Asia, Southeast Asia, Africa, Latin America)
Poor sanitation and unsafe drinking water
Consumption of street food or unhygienic food
Lack of vaccination before travel to high-risk areas
diagnosis_methods: Blood culture (most accurate in first week)
Bone marrow culture (most sensitive but invasive)
Widal test (serological test — less reliable due to false positives)
Typhidot or Tubex test (rapid antibody detection)
Complete blood count (shows low white blood cells and platelets)
treatment_options: Antibiotic therapy is the mainstay of treatment
Hospitalization for severe cases or complications
Supportive care including fever management and rest
Surgery in rare cases of intestinal perforation
medications: Ciprofloxacin or Ofloxacin (fluoroquinolones) — first-line in many areas (if sensitive)
Azithromycin — preferred in areas with fluoroquinolone resistance
Ceftriaxone (third-generation cephalosporin) — injectable, used for severe cases
Meropenem or Imipenem — for extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains
lifestyle_home_remedies: Complete bed rest during the acute phase
Drink plenty of clean fluids (boiled water, oral rehydration solution)
Use cool sponging to reduce high fever
diet_recommended: Soft, easily digestible foods (khichdi, porridge, bananas, rice, boiled potatoes)
Yogurt and buttermilk (probiotics help restore gut flora)
Coconut water and oral rehydration solutions
diet_to_avoid: High-fiber foods during acute phase (can irritate intestines)
summary_profile.when_to_see_doctor: Seek medical attention immediately if you have persistent high fever for more than 3–4 days, especially after returning from a high-risk area, along with headache, abdominal pain, or weakness. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent complications.
emergency_signs: Persistent vomiting preventing intake of fluids
Confusion, drowsiness, or loss of consciousness
Signs of shock (cold clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, low blood pressure)
